questions.q: What kind of course is Engineering 502 B, Calculus Two?
options: A Brief course: an overview of about five minutes and six lectures of about ten minutes, the second mathematics Foundations course in Anderson Engineering
An optional elective outside the Foundations
questions.explain:
Paragraph 0.1: Paragraph 0.1 gives the format and its place in the Foundations.
A is wrong: A Brief course is a first hour, not a substitute for a semester.
C is wrong: It is a Foundations course in Anderson Engineering.
D is wrong: It is a mathematics course.

questions.q: Which later course does the overview say depends on these ideas when it writes Gauss's law and Faraday's law?
questions.explain:
Paragraph 0.4: The overview names Physics Two as the course that uses gradients, flux, divergence, and curl.
A is wrong: Calculus One comes before this course.
C is wrong: Physics One treats mechanics, before Physics Two.
D is wrong: That is Course Zero, How to Use the Engineering Courses.

questions.q: Which MIT OpenCourseWare subject is the backbone of this course?
options: 18.02SC Multivariable Calculus, Fall 2010, taught by Professor Denis Auroux
questions.explain:
Paragraph 0.9: The overview credits 18.02SC and its supporting materials, published under a Creative Commons licence.
A is wrong: That is the backbone of Calculus One.
B is wrong: That is an MIT physics subject, not a mathematics subject.
C is wrong: That is a different MIT subject.

questions.q: What is the length of the vector A = a₁ i + a₂ j + a₃ k?
questions.explain:
Paragraph 1.2: The length comes from the Pythagorean theorem used twice.
B is wrong: Lengths come from squares, not a plain sum.
C is wrong: This omits the square root.
D is wrong: A product of components is not a length.

questions.q: Two nonzero vectors are perpendicular exactly when what is true?
questions.explain:
Paragraph 1.4: The dot product equals |A||B| cos θ, and cos 90° = 0.
B is wrong: A zero cross product means the vectors are parallel.
C is wrong: Length says nothing about angle.
D is wrong: That depends on their lengths; perpendicular needs zero.

questions.q: A constant force F acts along a displacement d. What work does it do?
options: F · d, the dot product of force and displacement
The determinant of F and d
questions.explain:
Paragraph 1.5: Only the component of force along the motion does work, which the dot product picks out.
A is wrong: That is a vector, and it is the form used for torque, not work.
C is wrong: The cosine of the angle matters; a sideways force does no work.
D is wrong: A determinant gives an area, not work.

questions.q: What is the determinant of the 2 × 2 array with rows (a, b) and (c, d)?
questions.explain:
Paragraph 1.6: Its absolute value is the area of the parallelogram spanned by the rows.
A is wrong: The products pair the diagonals, a with d and b with c.
B is wrong: This pairs the wrong entries.
D is wrong: The second product is subtracted.

questions.q: What is the length of the cross product A × B?
options: |A||B| sin θ, the area of the parallelogram A and B span
questions.explain:
Paragraph 1.7: The cross product's length is the parallelogram's area, and its direction is perpendicular to both vectors.
A is wrong: That is the dot product.
B is wrong: Lengths do not simply add in a product.
C is wrong: It is zero only for parallel vectors.

questions.q: What is B × A in terms of A × B?
options: −(A × B): reversing the order reverses the sign
questions.explain:
Paragraph 1.8: The cross product is anti-commutative, so order matters.
A is wrong: That would make the cross product commutative, which it is not.
B is wrong: That is the dot product, a scalar.
C is wrong: Only parallel vectors give zero.

questions.q: For A = (1, 2, 0) and B = (3, 1, 0), what is A × B?
options: (0, 0, −5), pointing straight down the z axis
questions.explain:
Paragraph 1.9: The k component is 1·1 − 2·3 = −5; the i and j components are zero because both vectors lie in the xy plane.
B is wrong: The sign is wrong: 1·1 − 2·3 is −5.
C is wrong: 5 is the dot product; the cross product is a vector.
D is wrong: That is the componentwise product, which is not the cross product.

questions.q: When does a square matrix A have an inverse?
options: Exactly when its determinant is not zero
Whenever all its entries are positive
Only when it is the identity matrix
Exactly when its determinant is zero
questions.explain:
Paragraph 1.11: Then A x = b has the single solution x = A⁻¹b.
B is wrong: Positive entries do not guarantee a non-zero determinant.
C is wrong: Many matrices have inverses.
D is wrong: Zero determinant means no inverse.

questions.q: If a 3 × 3 matrix A has determinant zero, what can be said about A x = b?
options: It always has exactly one solution
It has either no solution or infinitely many
questions.explain:
Paragraph 1.12: Zero determinant means the rows lie in one plane, so the system is degenerate.
A is wrong: That is the case when the determinant is not zero.
C is wrong: Linear systems never have exactly two solutions.
D is wrong: A has no inverse when its determinant is zero.

questions.q: What determines a plane in space, in the lecture's description?
options: A single direction vector lying in the plane
One point on the plane and a normal vector perpendicular to it
Its distance from the origin alone
questions.explain:
Paragraph 2.2: A point P lies on the plane exactly when the vector from P₀ to P is perpendicular to N.
A is wrong: Two points fix only a line.
B is wrong: Infinitely many planes contain a given direction.
D is wrong: Many planes share the same distance from the origin.

questions.q: How do you find a normal vector to the plane through three given points?
options: Take the dot product of two of the points
Form two vectors from one point to the other two and take their cross product
questions.explain:
Paragraph 2.3: The cross product is perpendicular to both vectors, and so to the plane.
A is wrong: The sum is not perpendicular to the plane in general.
B is wrong: A dot product is a number, not a vector.
C is wrong: That gives a point, not a normal direction.

questions.q: How is a line in space written parametrically?
options: a x + b y + c z = d
P₀ + t v, a point plus a multiple of a direction vector
questions.explain:
Paragraph 2.4: As t runs through the real numbers, the point moves along the line.
A is wrong: That single equation describes a plane.
B is wrong: That is a circle or cylinder.
C is wrong: That is the plane equation from a normal vector.

questions.q: What is the speed of a moving point along a curve r(t)?
options: The length of the velocity vector dr/dt
The length of the position vector
The length of the acceleration vector
The arc length divided by the radius
questions.explain:
Paragraph 2.7: Velocity is the derivative of position; its length is the speed ds/dt.
B is wrong: That is the distance from the origin.
C is wrong: Acceleration measures change of velocity.
D is wrong: That has no general meaning as speed.

questions.q: For uniform motion on a circle of radius a with angular speed ω, what is the acceleration?
options: Zero, because the speed is constant
It points along the velocity with size a ω
It points away from the centre with size ω
It points toward the centre with size a ω², the speed squared over the radius
questions.explain:
Paragraph 2.9: Differentiating twice gives −ω² times the position vector.
A is wrong: The direction of the velocity is turning, so acceleration is not zero.
B is wrong: a ω is the speed, and the acceleration is perpendicular to the velocity.
C is wrong: It points inward, and its size is a ω².

questions.q: If a vector function has constant length, how is its derivative related to it?
options: The derivative is perpendicular to the vector
The derivative is parallel to the vector
The derivative has the same length
questions.explain:
Paragraph 2.10: Differentiating r · r = constant with the product rule gives 2 r · r′ = 0.
B is wrong: Parallel change would alter the length.
C is wrong: The vector can turn while keeping its length.
D is wrong: Nothing forces equal lengths.

questions.q: What does Kepler's second law follow from, in the lecture's vector account?
options: The dot product of position and velocity is zero
The cross product of position and velocity is constant under a force directed toward the Sun
The speed of the planet is constant
questions.explain:
Paragraph 2.11: Half its length is the rate of sweeping out area, so equal areas are swept in equal times.
A is wrong: That would mean a circular orbit only.
C is wrong: Planets move faster when nearer the Sun.
D is wrong: Gravity accelerates the planet toward the Sun.

questions.q: What does a topographic map of a mountain draw?
options: Level curves, where the height takes a constant value
questions.explain:
Paragraph 3.2: Level curves are often more useful than the graph surface itself.
A is wrong: Gradients are perpendicular to the contours, not the contours themselves.
C is wrong: Those are slices, not level curves.
D is wrong: Those cross the level curves at right angles.

questions.q: What is the partial derivative ∂f/∂x?
options: The ordinary derivative of f in x while the other variables are held constant
The derivative of f along the steepest direction
The total change in f over a region
The derivative with all variables changing at once
questions.explain:
Paragraph 3.3: Geometrically it is the slope of the surface as you walk in the x direction.
B is wrong: That is the length of the gradient.
C is wrong: That is an integral, not a derivative.
D is wrong: A partial derivative changes one variable at a time.

questions.q: A plate measured as 2 m by 3 m has a 1 cm error in each side. About how much does the area estimate change?
questions.explain:
Paragraph 3.5: ΔA ≈ y Δx + x Δy = 3(0.01) + 2(0.01) = 0.05 m².
A is wrong: That is only the product of the two small errors, which the linear estimate ignores.
B is wrong: The partials are 3 and 2, not 3 and 3.
D is wrong: The decimal place is off by a factor of ten.

questions.q: For functions with continuous second partials, what is true of the mixed partials f_xy and f_yx?
options: They are equal, so the order of differentiation does not matter
questions.explain:
Paragraph 3.6: The lecture names this Clairaut's or Schwarz's theorem.
A is wrong: They are often non-zero.
C is wrong: They are equal, not opposite.
D is wrong: They exist for the smooth functions met in practice.

questions.q: What is z = x² − y² an example of at the origin?
options: A saddle: a critical point that is neither a maximum nor a minimum
A point where the partials are not zero
questions.explain:
Paragraph 3.7: Both partials are zero there, but the surface rises in one direction and falls in another.
A is wrong: It decreases along the y direction.
B is wrong: It increases along the x direction.
D is wrong: Both partials vanish at the origin.

questions.q: In the second derivative test, what does A C − B² < 0 mean at a critical point?
questions.explain:
Paragraph 3.8: A negative value of A C − B² means a saddle; a positive value means a maximum or minimum, decided by the sign of A.
A is wrong: That needs A C − B² > 0 and A > 0.
B is wrong: That needs A C − B² > 0 and A < 0.
D is wrong: That is the case when A C − B² = 0.

questions.q: For an open-topped box of fixed volume using the least material, what shape does the lecture find?
options: A square base with height equal to twice the side
A very flat box with tiny height
A square base with height half the side of the base
questions.explain:
Paragraph 3.10: Setting both partial derivatives of the area to zero gives that proportion.
A is wrong: A cube is best for a closed box, not an open-topped one.
B is wrong: The height is half the side, not twice it.
C is wrong: That uses too much material in the base.

questions.q: How does 18.02 present the method of least squares?
options: As a Lagrange multiplier problem with a circle constraint
As a double integral over the data
As finding where the data cross zero
As a minimum problem: choose slope and intercept to minimise the sum of squared vertical errors
questions.explain:
Paragraph 3.11: Setting the two partial derivatives of that sum to zero gives the best-fit line.
A is wrong: No constraint is involved.
B is wrong: Least squares minimises a sum, not an integral.
C is wrong: It fits a line, not roots.

questions.q: What is the gradient of f(x, y) = x² + y² at the point (x, y)?
options: (2x, 2y), pointing straight away from the origin
questions.explain:
Paragraph 4.2: The gradient's components are the partial derivatives f_x and f_y.
A is wrong: Those are the terms, not their derivatives.
C is wrong: The gradient is a vector, not a sum.
D is wrong: The components are swapped.

questions.q: In vector form, what is the rate of change of f along a moving point?
options: The gradient crossed with the velocity
The sum of the partial derivatives
The gradient of f dotted with the velocity vector
The length of the velocity alone
questions.explain:
Paragraph 4.3: That is the multivariable chain rule: df/dt = ∇f · dr/dt.
A is wrong: The chain rule uses a dot product.
B is wrong: The partials must be weighted by the rates dx/dt, dy/dt, dz/dt.
D is wrong: That is the speed, not the rate of change of f.

questions.q: How is the gradient related to the level curves and level surfaces of f?
options: It is parallel to the z axis
It has no fixed relation to them
questions.explain:
Paragraph 4.4: Along a level set f does not change, so the gradient dotted with any tangent velocity is zero.
A is wrong: Moving along a level set gives zero rate of change, so the gradient cannot point that way.
B is wrong: The gradient lies in the domain, not along the height axis.
C is wrong: The chain rule gives a definite relation.

questions.q: In which direction is the directional derivative of f largest?
options: Along the gradient, where it equals the length of the gradient
questions.explain:
Paragraph 4.5: The directional derivative is |∇f| cos of the angle, largest when the angle is zero.
A is wrong: There the directional derivative is zero.
B is wrong: That is the direction of fastest decrease.
C is wrong: The best direction depends on the function and the point.

questions.q: What condition does the method of Lagrange multipliers impose to find extremes of f subject to g = constant?
questions.explain:
Paragraph 4.8: At a constrained extreme, the gradient of f is a multiple of the gradient of g.
B is wrong: That ignores the constraint and finds unconstrained critical points.
C is wrong: The gradients are parallel, not perpendicular.
D is wrong: The method compares gradients, not function values.

questions.q: What point on the line x + y = 1 is closest to the origin?
questions.explain:
Paragraph 4.10: Lagrange's condition gives x = y, and the constraint then gives x = y = 1/2.
A is wrong: That point is on the line but at distance 1.
C is wrong: The origin is not on the line.
D is wrong: That point is not on the line.

questions.q: What does the Lagrange multiplier λ measure?
options: The distance to the constraint curve
How fast the optimal value of f changes as the constraint constant changes
questions.explain:
Paragraph 4.11: In economics it is a shadow price; in engineering, the rate of improvement as a budget is relaxed.
A is wrong: λ is a rate of change, not a distance.
B is wrong: λ is not a count.
D is wrong: The curl of a gradient is always zero.

questions.q: What is the volume under z = x + y over the unit square 0 ≤ x, y ≤ 1?
questions.explain:
Paragraph 5.4: The inner integral gives x + 1/2, and integrating that from 0 to 1 gives 1/2 + 1/2 = 1.
A is wrong: That is only half the answer: it forgets one of the two equal contributions.
B is wrong: The integrand averages to 1 over the square, so the volume is 1.
D is wrong: That is not the value of the iterated integral.

questions.q: What is the small area element in polar coordinates?
questions.explain:
Paragraph 5.5: A small polar box has sides dr and r dθ.
A is wrong: This omits the factor r, the most common error.
C is wrong: The extra factor is r, not r².
D is wrong: The conversion multiplies by r; it does not divide.

questions.q: In a general change of variables, how does the area element dx dy transform?
options: It becomes the absolute value of the Jacobian determinant times du dv
It becomes the gradient times du dv
questions.explain:
Paragraph 5.6: The Jacobian is the determinant of the partial derivatives of x and y with respect to u and v; for polar coordinates it gives r.
A is wrong: Areas stretch under a change of variables.
B is wrong: Area elements multiply, not add.
D is wrong: The factor is a determinant, not a gradient.

questions.q: How is the work done by a force field along a curve computed?
options: As the line integral of F · dr along the curve
As the double integral of F over the region
As the length of the curve times |F|
As the divergence of F at the endpoint
questions.explain:
Paragraph 5.9: Cut the curve into small steps, dot the force with each displacement, and add.
B is wrong: Work is a line integral along a path.
C is wrong: Only the component of force along the path counts.
D is wrong: Divergence measures spreading, not work.

questions.q: When is a vector field conservative, or path independent?
options: Only when it is zero everywhere
Exactly when it is the gradient of a potential function
questions.explain:
Paragraph 5.10: Then the work along any path is the difference of the potential between the endpoints.
A is wrong: Zero divergence is about sources and sinks, not path independence.
B is wrong: Constant magnitude does not make work path independent.
C is wrong: Many non-zero fields, such as gravity, are conservative.

questions.q: In a simply connected region, what test shows that M i + N j is a gradient field?
questions.explain:
Paragraph 5.11: The difference of those partials is the curl in the plane; zero curl in a region with no holes means conservative.
A is wrong: That compares the wrong partials.
B is wrong: Equal components do not make a field conservative.
D is wrong: That is zero divergence, not zero curl.

questions.q: Using Green's theorem, what is the circulation of −y i + x j around the unit circle?
options: 2π, because the curl is 2 and the disc's area is π
questions.explain:
Paragraph 5.12: The double integral of the curl, 2, over the unit disc equals 2π, matching the direct line integral.
A is wrong: This forgets that the curl is 2, not 1.
B is wrong: The field circulates, so the circulation is not zero.
D is wrong: The area of the unit disc is π, not 2π.

questions.q: In the flux form of Green's theorem, what is integrated over the region?
questions.explain:
Paragraph 5.13: The outward flux across a closed curve equals the double integral of the divergence inside.
A is wrong: That is the circulation form.
C is wrong: Green's theorem integrates a scalar quantity.
D is wrong: Area appears only when the divergence is constant.

questions.q: What volume element do cylindrical coordinates use?
options: ρ² sin φ dρ dφ dθ
questions.explain:
Paragraph 6.3: Cylindrical coordinates combine polar r and θ with height z.
B is wrong: This omits the factor r.
C is wrong: That is the spherical element.
D is wrong: The factor is r, not r².

questions.q: What is the volume element in spherical coordinates?
options: ρ² sin φ dρ dφ dθ
ρ² cos φ dρ dφ dθ
questions.explain:
Paragraph 6.4: Spherical coordinates use ρ, φ from the positive z axis, and θ; the element carries ρ² sin φ.
B is wrong: That resembles the cylindrical factor r, not the spherical one.
C is wrong: This omits the Jacobian factor.
D is wrong: With φ measured from the z axis, the factor is sin φ.

questions.q: What is the outward flux of F = x i + y j + z k through the sphere of radius a?
questions.explain:
Paragraph 6.6: On the sphere F · n = a, and multiplying by the surface area 4π a² gives 4π a³.
B is wrong: That is the surface area alone; F · n equals a, not 1.
C is wrong: That is the volume of the ball, not the flux.
D is wrong: The field points outward everywhere, so the flux is positive.

questions.q: What does the divergence of a field measure at a point?
options: The local rotation of the field
The net outflow per unit volume, how much the point acts as a source or sink
The work done around a closed loop
questions.explain:
Paragraph 6.7: Divergence is ∂P/∂x + ∂Q/∂y + ∂R/∂z, the local rate of spreading out.
A is wrong: That is the curl.
C is wrong: That is circulation, a line integral.
D is wrong: That is the gradient of a scalar function.

questions.q: What does the divergence theorem state?
options: The circulation around a curve equals the flux of the curl
The work along a path equals the potential difference
The divergence of a curl is always one
The outward flux through a closed surface equals the triple integral of the divergence over the solid inside
questions.explain:
Paragraph 6.8: It is also called Gauss's theorem, and it underlies Gauss's law in Physics Two.
A is wrong: That is Stokes' theorem.
B is wrong: That is the gradient theorem for line integrals.
C is wrong: The divergence of a curl is always zero.

questions.q: What does Stokes' theorem relate?
options: The flux through a closed surface and the divergence inside
The circulation around a closed curve and the flux of the curl through any surface bounded by it
A function on an interval and its endpoint values only
The gradient and the level surfaces
questions.explain:
Paragraph 6.10: Orientations match by the right-hand rule, and in the plane it reduces to Green's theorem.
A is wrong: That is the divergence theorem.
C is wrong: That is the one-variable Fundamental Theorem.
D is wrong: That is a property of gradients, not Stokes' theorem.

questions.q: What single story do the integral theorems of the course tell?
options: Integrating a derivative over a region equals integrating the original quantity over the boundary
questions.explain:
Paragraph 6.11: The Fundamental Theorem, the gradient theorem, Green's, Stokes', and the divergence theorem all share this form.
A is wrong: Many fields have non-zero curl.
B is wrong: The theorems are precisely about boundaries.
D is wrong: They are inverse processes, linked by these theorems.

questions.q: Which two identities follow from the equality of mixed partial derivatives?
options: The curl of a gradient is zero, and the divergence of a curl is zero
The gradient of a curl is zero, and the curl of a divergence is zero
The divergence of a gradient is always zero
The curl of any field is zero
questions.explain:
Paragraph 6.12: These identities are used repeatedly in electricity and magnetism.
B is wrong: Those expressions are not the standard identities.
C is wrong: That is the Laplacian, which is generally non-zero.
D is wrong: Only gradient fields have zero curl.
